questions.q: According to Bayes' theorem, the posterior P(θ | D) is proportional to which product?
options: The prior times the sample size
The likelihood P(D | θ) times the prior P(θ)
The variance times the mean
The confidence level times the standard error
questions.explain: Bayes' theorem gives P(θ|D) = P(D|θ)P(θ)/P(D), so the posterior is proportional to likelihood × prior, with P(D) acting only as a normalizing constant.

questions.q: A trading strategy's win rate has a Beta(1, 1) prior. After observing 8 wins and 2 losses, what is the posterior distribution?
options: Beta(8, 2)
Beta(9, 3)
Beta(1, 1)
Beta(2, 8)
questions.explain: The Beta-Binomial update adds observed wins to α and losses to β: posterior = Beta(α + wins, β + losses) = Beta(1+8, 1+2) = Beta(9, 3).

questions.q: In the Normal-Normal conjugate model, as the number of data points n grows very large, what happens to the posterior mean μ_post?
options: It stays fixed at the prior mean μ₀ forever
It converges toward the sample mean x̄, since the data's precision dominates the prior's precision
It becomes undefined
It converges to zero regardless of the data
questions.explain: The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and sample mean. As n grows, the data's precision (n/σ²) dominates the prior's fixed precision (1/τ₀²), pulling μ_post toward x̄.

questions.q: What is the key difference in meaning between a Bayesian 95% credible interval and a frequentist 95% confidence interval?
options: There is no difference; they always mean exactly the same thing
A credible interval makes a direct probability statement about θ given the observed data, while a confidence interval describes the long-run coverage rate of the procedure across repeated samples
A confidence interval only applies to discrete data
A credible interval requires an infinite sample size to compute
questions.explain: A credible interval says 'given this data, there's a 95% probability θ is in this range.' A confidence interval says 'if I repeated this procedure many times, 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true θ' — it treats θ as fixed and the interval as random, not the other way around.

questions.q: Why is the Beta distribution called a 'conjugate prior' for binomial data?
options: Because it always has a mean of 0.5
Because the posterior distribution, after combining a Beta prior with binomial data, is itself a Beta distribution
Because it can only be used with normally distributed data
Because it eliminates the need for a likelihood function
questions.explain: A conjugate prior is one where the resulting posterior stays within the same distributional family as the prior. For binomial data, a Beta prior always yields a Beta posterior, turning the Bayesian update into simple parameter arithmetic.
